source.title: Complex Visual Adaptations in Squid for Specific Tasks in Different Environments

method: histology: longitudinal sections of the retina (Figure 4A)
conditions: Coastal squid collected by seine net at Moreton Bay, Queensland, 2010; mantle length 8 to 14 mm; number of sectioned animals not stated in the sentence
quote: Longitudinal sections of I. notoides retina (the red dash line in Figure 4A) showed a variance of rhabdom width between 4 and 7 μm.
note: Licence: the version of record's own XML file on Frontiers (public-pages-files-2025.frontiersin.org) states CC BY 4.0 (creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); the Crossref record read through WebFetch carried no licence entry, so the licence rests on the publisher file. The paper prints the name Idiosepius notoides; GBIF lists it as a SYNONYM of Xipholeptos notoides (S.S.Berry, 1921), the accepted name, family Idiosepiidae, order Idiosepida, so it is filed under the accepted name. Specimens: Moreton Bay, Queensland, 2010, seine net, mantle length 8 to 14 mm; Table 1 lists 6 histology specimens, but no sentence says how many were sectioned for this result. The Methods say the individual with the highest MRI voxel resolution in each species was selected for the quantitative analysis of eyes and brain lobes, so the optical calculations rest on one individual. Crossref gives volume 8 and no issue or article number. The sentence gives a range of rhabdom width from sections cut along the red dashed line in Figure 4A; it does not say whether the range lies within one eye or across eyes. The next sentence in the paper reports a thin (4 um) and long (200 um) rhabdom patch in the dorso-posterior retina.

source.title: Complex Visual Adaptations in Squid for Specific Tasks in Different Environments

value: patch of thin (4 um) and long (200 um) rhabdoms in the dorso-posterior retina, with high visual resolution if photoreceptors are not coupled
method: histology of retina sections; resolution inferred from rhabdom dimensions
conditions: Coastal squid collected by seine net at Moreton Bay, Queensland, 2010; mantle length 8 to 14 mm; the high-resolution reading holds only 'assuming no photoreceptor coupling'
quote: A thin (4 μm) and long rhabdom (200 μm) patch in this species in the dorso-posterior retina results in corresponding high visual resolution, assuming no photoreceptor coupling.
note: Licence: the version of record's own XML file on Frontiers (public-pages-files-2025.frontiersin.org) states CC BY 4.0 (creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); the Crossref record read through WebFetch carried no licence entry, so the licence rests on the publisher file. The paper prints the name Idiosepius notoides; GBIF lists it as a SYNONYM of Xipholeptos notoides (S.S.Berry, 1921), the accepted name, family Idiosepiidae, order Idiosepida, so it is filed under the accepted name. Specimens: Moreton Bay, Queensland, 2010, seine net, mantle length 8 to 14 mm; Table 1 lists 6 histology specimens, but no sentence says how many were sectioned for this result. The Methods say the individual with the highest MRI voxel resolution in each species was selected for the quantitative analysis of eyes and brain lobes, so the optical calculations rest on one individual. The authors do not call the patch a fovea in this sentence; the next sentence says 'This forward-looking area, like the foveal regions in fish, is likely used in predation (Figure 4).' source.title: Complex Visual Adaptations in Squid for Specific Tasks in Different Environments

method: calculated (anatomical): spatial resolution R = f/2p (Equation 3), p the centre-to-centre receptor separation, from MRI and histology dimensions; the paper prints cycles per radian
conditions: Optical properties calculated for one individual (the animal with the highest MRI voxel resolution); wavelength 500 nm for coastal species; not a behavioural measurement
quote: Angular image size and the resolving power per receptor were significantly influenced by the size of aperture, therefore, the tiny I. notoides has the lowest angular image size (0.00086 radians) and spatial resolution (92.5 cycles radian−1).
note: Licence: the version of record's own XML file on Frontiers (public-pages-files-2025.frontiersin.org) states CC BY 4.0 (creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/); the Crossref record read through WebFetch carried no licence entry, so the licence rests on the publisher file. The paper prints the name Idiosepius notoides; GBIF lists it as a SYNONYM of Xipholeptos notoides (S.S.Berry, 1921), the accepted name, family Idiosepiidae, order Idiosepida, so it is filed under the accepted name. Specimens: Moreton Bay, Queensland, 2010, seine net, mantle length 8 to 14 mm; Table 1 lists 6 histology specimens, but no sentence says how many were sectioned for this result. The Methods say the individual with the highest MRI voxel resolution in each species was selected for the quantitative analysis of eyes and brain lobes, so the optical calculations rest on one individual. Crossref gives volume 8 and no issue or article number. Conversion: the paper prints 92.5 cycles per radian; 92.5 / 57.2958 = 1.61 cycles per degree. This is a calculated optical limit, not a measured acuity. The text I read does not state p; Table 3 (read through WebFetch) lists focal length 740 um and receptor diameter 4 um, and 740 / (2 x 4) = 92.5, so p appears to be the 4 um receptor diameter (my inference). The printed angular image size of 0.00086 radians does not follow from Equation 2 (1.22 x wavelength / aperture) with 500 nm and the Table 3 aperture of 580 um, which gives about 0.00105 radians (my arithmetic); the paper does not explain the gap, so the printed figures need caution. The sentence says 'significantly' with no test named.
